title: Tiles, Windows, Headings, Raw Input & States
description: Truchet tiles, layouts that read the window state, one selector for six heading levels, raw pointer samples, self-declaring components.

drops.title: Truchet Weave
drops.description: One asymmetric tile, rotated at random, knits an endless maze — then re-knits as flips travel through the grid.
drops.concept: The Smith tile — two diametrically opposed quarter-circles — is the cheapest trick in generative art: tile a grid with random rotations and the arcs join across every cell boundary into long continuous curves. Animating the rotations turns the static pattern into cloth being rewoven, and three choreographies (a diagonal wave, expanding ripples, random twinkle) plus four motifs show how far one tile stretches.
drops.source: Rombo's Truchet pattern write-up (after Truchet 1704 / Cyril Stanley Smith 1987)

interaction.mouse: Moving the pointer flips the tiles it crosses; the trio below runs three different choreographies at once.
interaction.click: Tap the big panel to send a ripple of flips outward; the panel tunes grid, stroke, wave speed, motif and mode.
interaction.touch: Drag to flip tiles, tap to ripple; the control panel stacks above the canvas on narrow screens.

drops.title: Window States
drops.description: display-state asks the window manager, not the viewport — so the rail widens when maximized and the chrome leaves in fullscreen.
drops.concept: Every responsive layout asks how wide it is, but a maximized window and a hand-dragged window of the same width are different rooms. The display-state media feature (with its companion resizable) reports the OS-level window state — normal, minimized, maximized, fullscreen — so an app shell can recompose rather than merely reflow. Native media queries drive it where supported, and a simulated mirror shows the same layout everywhere.
drops.source: W3C Window Management spec — display-state & resizable media features, shipping in Chrome 155

interaction.mouse: Pick a window state in the panel and the shell, rail, inspector and both mini windows recompose together.
interaction.click: 'Real fullscreen' enters the actual fullscreen state so the native media query fires; the badge says whether the feature is native or simulated.
interaction.touch: Same buttons; the panel moves inline above the demo on small screens.

drops.title: One Selector, Six Levels
drops.description: The :heading pseudo-class styles h1–h6 and role=heading alike, so an entire type scale fits in six rules.
drops.concept: Safari 27 shipped :heading and its functional :heading(1,2) form. Instead of repeating h1,h2,h3,h4,h5,h6 in every selector list, the whole hierarchy comes from one block driven by a base size and a ratio — and because the selector follows heading semantics rather than tag names, a div with role=heading aria-level=3 picks up exactly the level-3 styling. Three documents share the rules; four presets and five dials reshape all of them at once.
drops.source: CSS-Tricks almanac entry for the :heading pseudo-class (Safari 27)

interaction.mouse: Drag the base size, scale ratio, weight, tracking and hue dials; every heading in all three documents responds.
interaction.click: Four scale presets (editorial, compact, poster, humanist) reset the whole hierarchy at once.
interaction.touch: All dials are sliders; the panel sits above the documents on narrow screens.

drops.title: Raw Input
drops.description: pointermove against pointerrawupdate with getCoalescedEvents unpacked — every sample the digitiser produced.
drops.concept: pointerrawupdate fires as often as the browser can produce it, while pointermove is throttled toward the frame; neither is more precise, raw is just more of it sooner. Dragging across both panes shows the difference as events per second, samples per second and the average gap in milliseconds — and a fake main-thread load slider makes the throttled trail visibly cut corners while the raw trail keeps its samples.

interaction.mouse: Drag across both panes and compare the live counters; the signature pad below switches between raw samples and move-only.
interaction.click: Toggle raw/move on the pad, clear it, and dial in trail life, sample dots and fake main-thread load.
interaction.touch: Touch drags are sampled the same way — a finger usually produces more raw samples than a mouse.

drops.title: States From Inside
drops.description: Custom elements publish busy, done and error through ElementInternals.states; the page styles them with :state().
drops.concept: A component knows things the page does not — that it is uploading, that the last attempt failed, that the user already voted. CustomStateSet turns those facts into real CSS state, so :state(busy) styles them from outside the shadow boundary with no class juggling and no reaching in. Three elements (uploader, track, vote) drive themselves through idle/busy/done/error, a live inspector prints each element's state set, and an :is() wrapper keeps the same stylesheet working where :state() is not understood.
drops.source: Danny Moerkerke on the hidden power of custom states for web components

interaction.mouse: Drive each element with its buttons — upload, make it fail, play, buffer, vote, reject — and watch the outside styling follow.
interaction.click: Every state change re-renders the CustomStateSet inspector at the bottom of the page.
interaction.touch: All controls are ordinary buttons; the three components stack on narrow screens.
